"use server";

import { revalidatePath } from "next/cache";
import { VPS_TERMS } from "./billing-terms";
import { db } from "./db";
import { requireArea } from "./rbac";
import { SETTINGS_DEFAULTS } from "./settings";
import { encryptSecret } from "./crypto-box";

/**
 * Server actions for the admin settings hub. One entry point, `saveSettings`,
 * writes the rows for a single section (tab). Which keys belong to a section —
 * and how each is coerced — is described declaratively below so the action never
 * trusts the client for the key list.
 *
 * Coercion rules:
 *  - "bool":   checkbox → "true"/"false" (unchecked checkboxes don't POST, so we
 *              can't rely on presence alone; every bool key is always written).
 *  - "int":    trimmed, validated integer, range-checked; blank restores the default.
 *  - "num":    same as "int" but decimals are kept (percent fields).
 *  - "enum":   must be one of `values`; anything else is refused.
 *  - "secret": only written when non-blank, so a blank field never wipes the
 *              stored secret — and stored secrets are never echoed to the client.
 *  - "string": trimmed as-is.
 *
 * WHY THE RANGES AND THE "enum" TYPE EXIST
 * ----------------------------------------
 * Every numeric field on this page is a free-text box that an operator types into
 * once, at speed, usually during an incident — and several of them multiply money
 * or gate an irreversible action. The two failures this codebase has already shipped
 * were both of exactly this shape: `domain_markup_percent` billed a hardcoded 25%
 * while the panel showed 0%, and the auto-suspend kill switch reported "Saved." and
 * then let the sweep take customer VMs offline anyway. Both were silent.
 *
 * So values are validated HERE, at the write, and an out-of-range entry is REFUSED
 * with a message naming the allowed range rather than quietly stored or quietly
 * clamped. Refusing is the honest option: the row that ends up in the database is
 * always exactly the number the operator can see in the field. Where a reader also
 * clamps (`lib/registrar.ts` domainMarkupPct, `worker/billing.ts` dunningConfig) the
 * bounds below are set to AGREE with it, so the panel can never display one number
 * while the platform enforces another — which is the whole defect class this page
 * keeps producing.
 *
 * `enum` matters for the same reason: a `<select>` constrains a browser, not a
 * request. A hand-crafted POST could otherwise store `currency: "'; DROP"` or a
 * `default_term` no charge path understands.
 */

type FieldType = "string" | "bool" | "int" | "num" | "secret" | "enum" | "json";
type Field = {
  key: string;
  type: FieldType;
  /** Inclusive bounds for "int"/"num". Out of range is refused, not clamped. */
  min?: number;
  max?: number;
  /** Permitted values for "enum". */
  values?: readonly string[];
};

const CURRENCIES = ["USD", "EUR", "GBP", "CAD", "AUD"] as const;

/**
 * Permitted `default_term` values: the MONTH COUNTS the platform actually sells, derived
 * from `VPS_TERMS` so this list cannot drift from the deploy wizard's own buttons.
 *
 * This was `["monthly", "quarterly", "annual"]` — the vocabulary the comment at the top of
 * this file warned about ("a `default_term` no charge path understands"). It was worse than
 * unreadable: "quarterly" names a term that does not exist anywhere in the catalogue, and
 * the enum could not express the 24- and 36-month terms that do. Storing months, validated
 * against the single source of truth, is what made wiring the setting possible at all.
 *
 * A legacy "monthly"/"annual" row is no longer accepted on write and is ignored on read —
 * `defaultTermMonths()` falls back to the first term rather than pre-selecting a
 * commitment `vpsTerm()` would silently reprice.
 */
const TERMS = VPS_TERMS.map((t) => String(t.months)) as readonly string[];

/**
 * Floor for `dunning_terminate_days`: the first day the billing sweep could ever
 * legitimately destroy a VM.
 *
 * Derived from `worker/billing.ts`, which will not terminate before
 * `CARD_SUSPEND_DAY + SUSPEND_SLIP_CAP_DAYS + 1` — today (2 × DUNNING_RETRY_ATTEMPTS
 * − 1) + 1 + 4 + 1 = 11, with DUNNING_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3 in `lib/mailer.ts`. Those
 * constants are module-private over there, so this cannot be imported; it is
 * duplicated deliberately and named so it is greppable if the retry schedule changes.
 *
 * It is enforced here so the panel cannot DISPLAY a termination day earlier than the
 * one the worker will actually honour. Drift is safe in one direction only: the
 * worker's own clamp merely raises `terminateDays`, so a stale floor here costs a
 * cosmetic mismatch, never a VM deleted early.
 */
const MIN_TERMINATE_DAYS = 11;

const SECTION_FIELDS: Record<string, Field[]> = {
  general: [
    { key: "brand_name", type: "string" },
    { key: "brand_tagline", type: "string" },
    { key: "support_email", type: "string" },
    { key: "company_legal_name", type: "string" },

lib/billing-terms.ts defines `export const DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT = 20;` (used as the fallback discountPct in the VPS_TERMS array for the 12-month "Annual" term). But a large number of tests across multiple files (test/billing-terms.test.ts, and cascading through anything that imports/uses annual-discount pricing — proration, resize, order, promo-window tests) still hardcode the expectation that this constant is `10`. Example: `test/billing-terms.test.ts`'s "vpsTerm returns the matching term by months" expects 10, gets 20. This produces a consistent pattern of "expected 10800, got 9600" / "expected 3596, got 3197" type failures — always a 2x-ish or proportional mismatch traceable to the 10-vs-20 discrepancy.

Separately, there IS a live-settings mechanism too: the `annual_discount_percent` Setting (read via `lib/annual-discount.ts`'s `annualDiscountPct()`) currently has no override row in the production DB, so it resolves to its SETTINGS_DEFAULTS fallback of "10" (see lib/settings.ts). That live/DB-backed path is UNRELATED to and currently disagrees with the DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT=20 code constant — worth understanding whether that's intentional (two independently-configurable "10 vs 20" defaults that happen to differ) or itself a bug, while you're in there.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

content.text:
Build succeeded (exit code 0, full production build including all admin routes, no compile/type errors). Everything is verified and committed.

## Summary

All work is committed to branch `feat/grandfathered-price-fleet-tags` in the isolated worktree `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather` (never touched live `/opt/nxeon`). Not pushed, not deployed.

**The field:** No new field was added. `Server.grandfatheredRenewalCents` already existed — a "grandfather program" (shipped 2026-09-17) that auto-freezes a server's renewal rate at sale/resize, already wired as the one override point inside `renewalCharge`. Adding a second field would have meant arbitrating between two "locked price" fields inside that one shared formula — exactly the ambiguity its own docstring warns against — so I reused it for the admin's manual "honor an old price" case too. This is the main judgment call: I verified nothing else close existed, confirmed the mechanism already matched the spec, and built the missing piece instead of a redundant one.

**How an admin sets it:** `/admin/servers/[id]` now has a "Renewal price" section showing the live catalog rate vs. the locked rate (if any), with a form to set or clear it (`adminSetGrandfatheredPrice`/`adminClearGrandfatheredPrice` in `lib/actions.ts`, `GrandfatheredPriceForm` in `components/SubscriptionControls.tsx`), audit-logged (`admin.set_grandfathered_price`/`admin.clear_grandfathered_price`) matching the existing `adminExtendServer`/`adminSetServerFree` pattern exactly.

**Critical bug found and fixed:** Auditing every real `renewalCharge`/`renewalQuote` caller (as instructed) turned up that `renewNow` (manual "Renew now", `lib/actions.ts`) built a fresh object that silently dropped `grandfatheredRenewalCents` (and `annualDiscountPct`) — unlike every other caller, which passes the raw `Server` row through. A read-only prod query found **26 live servers today** whose grandfathered rate already diverges from their live plan price; any of them clicking "Renew now" themselves would have been overcharged. Fixed, with a permanent source-level regression test.

**Fleet list fix:** `lib/admin-fleet.ts` adds `serverFleetPriceCents` (add-on- and override-aware, via `renewalCharge`) and `serverFleetTags` (Grandfathered / add-on tags / Renewing soon / Overdue / Deleting soon — every condition lifted verbatim from an existing real definition, not invented). Settings and dunning config are batch-fetched once per page load; per-row work is pure arithmetic, no N+1. `lib/dunning-config.ts` is a new shared home for `dunningConfig()` (moved out of `worker/billing.ts` behavior-preservingly) so "Deleting soon" uses the exact grace-period math the real sweep uses.

**Judgment calls:** "Renewing soon" reuses this same file's existing `EXPIRING_SOON_DAYS = 5` (not the 3-day dunning-warning window elsewhere) so the page's own banner and the new tag never disagree. "Deleting soon" replaces "Overdue" rather than showing both, since it's a strict subset. The price column doesn't zero out for suspended servers (unlike MRR's `serverMonthlyCents`) so it can sit meaningfully next to the "Overdue" tag instead of reading as "$0.00 owed."

**Verification:** Typecheck clean. Full test suite: 16 new tests, zero regressions (confirmed byte-identical 37 pre-existing failures before/after — an unrelated `DEFAULT_ANNUAL_DISCOUNT_PCT` drift, flagged as a separate task). Full production build succeeds. Read-only prod queries confirm `darkeden-guard-sg` now shows **$27.49/mo** ($24.99 grandfathered base + $2.50 for 25GB disk), matching the owner's own description exactly; no suspended/overdue servers currently exist in prod to cross-check Overdue/Deleting-soon against live data, so that logic is covered by tests mirroring `worker/billing.ts`'s exact definitions instead.

Key files: `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/lib/admin-fleet.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/lib/dunning-config.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/lib/actions.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/components/SubscriptionControls.tsx`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/app/admin/servers/page.tsx`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/app/admin/servers/[id]/page.tsx`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/worker/billing.ts`, `/opt/nxeon-work-grandfather/test/admin-fleet.test.ts`.

result: Built and committed (branch `feat/grandfathered-price-fleet-tags`, not pushed/deployed) a real admin-settable grandfathered-price mechanism (reusing the existing `Server.grandfatheredRenewalCents` field), fixed a live bug where manual "Renew now" ignored it, and rewired the admin fleet list's price column and new lifecycle tags (Grandfathered/add-ons/Renewing soon/Overdue/Deleting soon) through the one shared `renewalCharge` formula — verified clean on typecheck, full test suite (16 new tests, zero regressions), a full production build, and real read-only production data matching the owner's own numbers on `darkeden-guard-sg`.
